title: Power
lead: A rocket blasting off, a dragster leaving the starting line and a volcano throwing its lava into the atmosphere have one thing in common: each does a great deal of work in a very short time. That rate is what power measures. This section defines power as the work done divided by the time it takes, gives it the watt and sets the older horsepower beside it, works out the power a woman puts out running up a flight of stairs, and then turns the definition around to find the energy a household appliance uses over a month and what it costs to run.
objectives: Calculate power by calculating changes in energy over time.
Examine power consumption and calculations of the cost of energy consumed.
summary_html:
• Power is the rate at which work is done, or in equation form, for the average power $\kP$ for work $\kW$ done over a time $\kt$, $\kP = \kW/\kt$.
  • The SI unit for power is the watt (W), where $\text{1 W} = \text{1 J/s}$.
  • The power of many devices such as electric motors is also often expressed in horsepower (hp), where $\text{1 hp} = \text{746 W}$.

exercises.prompt: Most electrical appliances are rated in watts. Does this rating depend on how long the appliance is on? (When off, it is a zero-watt device.) Explain in terms of the definition of power.

answer.solution: No. Power is the rate at which work is done, $\kP = \kW/\kt$, so a watt is a joule every second rather than a quantity of energy. The rating says how fast the appliance takes energy from the supply while it is running, and that rate belongs to the appliance itself, so switching it on for a minute or for a month does not change it. What the time does change is the energy the appliance uses, $\kE = \kP\kt$, which is what the electricity company bills you for. A 60-W bulb takes 60 J every second whichever it is; only the total mounts up.

exercises.prompt: Explain, in terms of the definition of power, why energy consumption is sometimes listed in kilowatt-hours rather than joules. What is the relationship between these two energy units?

answer.solution: Since power is the rate at which energy is spent, the energy spent is the power multiplied by the time, $\kE = \kP\kt$, and any power unit multiplied by any time unit is therefore an energy unit. A kilowatt-hour is the energy a device drawing one kilowatt takes in one hour. Household appliances draw about a kilowatt and run for hours at a stretch, so a month of them comes to a few hundred kilowatt-hours, which is a convenient size of number to print on a bill. The same energy in joules would be unwieldy, because $1\ \text{kW}\cdot\text{h} = (1000\ \text{W})(3600\ \text{s}) = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}$, so every kilowatt-hour on the bill is three and a half million joules.

exercises.prompt: A spark of static electricity, such as that you might receive from a doorknob on a cold dry day, may carry a few hundred watts of power. Explain why you are not injured by such a spark.

answer.solution: A few hundred watts sounds alarming because it is the rate at which a bright lamp spends energy, but power is only a rate, and a spark lasts a very small fraction of a second. The energy that actually reaches you is $\kE = \kP\kt$, and with a time of the order of a microsecond a few hundred watts amounts to a small fraction of a joule, far too little to heat tissue or to do any damage, however sharp the shock feels. A rating in watts never settles on its own whether something is dangerous; you have to ask how long it goes on for as well.

exercises.prompt: The Crab Nebula (see the figure below) pulsar is the remnant of a supernova that occurred in A.D. 1054. Using data from Table 7.3, calculate the approximate factor by which the power output of this astronomical object has declined since its explosion.

answer.hint: Table 7.3 gives the power of a supernova at its peak and the power of the Crab Nebula pulsar today. The factor by which the output has declined is the second of these divided by the first.

exercises.prompt: A person in good physical condition can put out 100 W of useful power for several hours at a stretch, perhaps by pedaling a mechanism that drives an electric generator. Neglecting any problems of generator efficiency and practical considerations such as resting time: (a) How many people would it take to run a 4.00-kW electric clothes dryer? (b) How many people would it take to replace a large electric power plant that generates 800 MW?

parts.hint: Each person supplies 100 W, so divide the power the dryer needs by the power one person can put out.
One megawatt is $10^{6}\ \text{W}$, so write 800 MW in watts before dividing by the 100 W one person supplies.

exercises.prompt: A large household air conditioner may consume 15.0 kW of power. What is the cost of operating this air conditioner 3.00 h per day for 30.0 d if the cost of electricity is ＄0.110 per $\text{kW}\cdot\text{h}$?

answer.hint: Find the energy from $\kE = \kP\kt$ with the power in kilowatts and the time in hours, and then multiply that number of kilowatt-hours by the price of one.

exercises.prompt: (a) What is the average useful power output of a person who does $6.00 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}$ of useful work in 8.00 h? (b) Working at this rate, how long will it take this person to lift 2000 kg of bricks 1.50 m to a platform? (Work done to lift his body can be omitted because it is not considered useful output here.)

parts.hint: Put the time in seconds before dividing the work by it.

parts.part: the time to lift the bricks
parts.hint: The work needed is $m\kg\kh$ for the bricks, and the time is that work divided by the power found in (a).

exercises.prompt: (a) How long will it take an 850-kg car with a useful power output of 40.0 hp (1 hp = 746 W) to reach a speed of 15.0 m/s, neglecting friction? (b) How long will this acceleration take if the car also climbs a 3.00-m-high hill in the process?

parts.hint: The work the engine must do is the kinetic energy the car gains, and the time is that work divided by the power in watts.
Now the engine must supply the gravitational potential energy $m\kg\kh$ as well as the kinetic energy.

exercises.prompt: (a) What is the available energy content, in joules, of a battery that operates a 2.00-W electric clock for 18 months? (b) How long can a battery that can supply $8.00 \times 10^{4}\ \text{J}$ run a pocket calculator that consumes energy at the rate of $1.00 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{W}$?

parts.part: the energy in the clock battery
parts.hint: Use $\kE = \kP\kt$ with the time written in seconds.
Divide the energy by the power to get a time in seconds, and then turn that into years.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the power output needed for a 950-kg car to climb a $2.00^\circ$ slope at a constant 30.0 m/s while encountering wind resistance and friction totaling 600 N. Explicitly show how you follow the steps in the Problem-Solving Strategies for Energy.

answer.hint: At a constant speed the force the car applies must balance the resistive forces and the component of the weight along the slope, and the power is that force multiplied by the speed.
answer.solution: Identify knowns: $m = 950\ \text{kg}$, slope angle $\theta = 2.00^\circ$, $\kv = 3.00\ \text{m/s}$, $f = 600\ \text{N}$. Identify unknowns: power $\kP$ of the car, force $\kF$ that car applies to road. Solve for unknown: $$\kP = \frac{\kW}{\kt} = \frac{\kF\kd}{\kt} = \kF\left(\frac{\kd}{\kt}\right) = \kF\kv,$$ where $\kF$ is parallel to the incline and must oppose the resistive forces and the force of gravity: $$\kF = f + w = 600\ \text{N} + m\kg\sin\theta.$$ Insert this into the expression for power and solve: $$\begin{aligned}\kP &= (f + m\kg\sin\theta)\kv\\ &= (600\ \text{N} + (950\ \text{kg})(9.80\ \text{m/s}^2)\sin 2^\circ)(30.0\ \text{m/s})\\ &= 2.77 \times 10^{4}\ \text{W}.\end{aligned}$$ About 28 kW (or about 37 hp) is reasonable for a car to climb a gentle incline.
